issues.legal_issue: The statutory restriction on trustees’ dispositions of trust property does not invalidate a court sale in execution of a decree merely because the Charity Commissioner did not sanction the sale.
material_facts: The property sold in execution of a mortgage decree belonged to a public trust.
The sale was conducted by the executing court to recover a debt due under the mortgage decree, rather than voluntarily by the trustees.
issues.conclusion: The word “sale” in the statutory restriction on dispositions by trustees does not include a court sale in execution of a decree; the sale was not invalid for want of the Charity Commissioner’s prior sanction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act restricts voluntary transactions by trustees, including a transfer by trustees for a price, but does not restrict a civil court’s power to sell trust property in execution of a decree. The Court found no clear provision extending the restriction to court sales and relied on the provision’s language and context in the chapter on accounts and audit.

predicates.court_sale_in_execution: A court sold property in order to execute a decree.
predicates.property_belongs_to_public_trust: The property sold belonged to a public trust.

issues.definition: When a court sells property belonging to a public trust to execute a decree, the sale is not invalid merely for lack of sanction for a trustee’s disposition.

issues.legal_issue: Enforcement of a mortgage against property belonging to a public trust does not, by itself, make the proceeding one in which a question affecting a public religious or charitable purpose is involved.
material_facts: The proceeding sought to enforce a mortgage decree against property belonging to a public trust.
The proceeding concerned enforcement of the mortgage and did not involve a separate question affecting a public religious or charitable purpose.
issues.conclusion: The proceeding did not involve a question affecting a public religious or charitable purpose within the meaning of section 56B, so notice to the Charity Commissioner was not obligatory.
issues.legal_principle: Section 56B of the Bombay Public Trusts Act requires notice to the Charity Commissioner before a court determines a question affecting a public religious or charitable purpose. A suit to enforce a mortgage, or a proceeding to enforce a mortgage decree against trust property, is not on that account such a proceeding.

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_proceeding: The proceeding was brought to enforce a mortgage or a mortgage decree.
predicates.property_belongs_to_public_trust: The property against which enforcement was sought belonged to a public trust.

issues.definition: When a proceeding enforces a mortgage against property belonging to a public trust, notice is not required merely because of that enforcement.

issues.legal_issue: A sale in execution of a mortgage decree cannot be set aside under the applicable sale-setting-aside procedure when the required amount for the decree-holder remains unpaid, even if the decree-holder agrees to defer payment or abandon the execution proceeding.
material_facts: The trustees applied to set aside a court sale in execution of a mortgage decree.

They deposited five per cent of the purchase money for the auction purchaser but did not deposit the amount required for payment to the decree-holder; the amount they deposited did not satisfy the mortgagee’s claim.
The mortgagee had agreed to give the trustees time to pay and, in the meantime, to abandon the execution application.
issues.conclusion: The required deposit for the decree-holder was not made, and the mortgagee’s agreement to wait or abandon execution did not satisfy that requirement. The executing court therefore had no power to set aside the sale on the basis of the deposits made.
issues.legal_principle: Order 21, rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires both a deposit for the auction purchaser and payment to the decree-holder of the amount specified in the sale proclamation, less amounts received after the proclamation. Abandonment of execution does not extinguish the creditor’s claim, and an agreement to extend time while receiving interest is not equivalent to payment of the required amount. The Court noted decisions including Subbayya v. Venkata Subba Reddi, Muthuvenkatapathy Reddy v. Kuppu Reddi, Laxmansing Baliramsing v. Laxminarayan Deosthan, Rabindra Nath v. Harendra Kumar, and M. H. Shivaji Rao v. Niranjanaiah, but expressly left open whether they were correctly decided where the decree-holder’s claim is otherwise satisfied.

rule.if: application_to_set_aside_execution_sale and purchaser_compensation_deposited and decree_holder_amount_unpaid and creditor_agreed_to_defer_or_abandon_without_receiving_that_amount

predicates.application_to_set_aside_execution_sale: A person applied to set aside a sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.purchaser_compensation_deposited: The applicant deposited the amount intended to compensate the auction purchaser.
predicates.decree_holder_amount_unpaid: The amount required for payment to the decree-holder remained unpaid.
predicates.creditor_agreed_to_defer_or_abandon_with: The decree-holder agreed to wait for payment or abandon execution without receiving the required amount.

issues.definition: When an applicant seeks to set aside an execution sale, has compensated the purchaser, but has not paid the decree-holder’s required amount, an agreement to wait or abandon execution does not permit the sale to be set aside on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A single judge must follow an applicable precedent of a court of coordinate or superior authority and cannot disregard it on the basis of the judge’s view of the evidence law or judicial oath.
material_facts: A single judge declined to follow decisions of courts of coordinate or superior authority, including a Full Bench decision, and treated the Full Bench decision as having no legal existence.
The judge relied on the Evidence Act and the judicial oath as reasons for not being bound by precedent.
issues.conclusion: A single judge is ordinarily bound by applicable decisions of courts of coordinate jurisdiction, Division Benches, Full Benches, and the Supreme Court; reliance on the Evidence Act or the judicial oath does not justify ignoring that rule.
issues.legal_principle: The binding force of precedent serves uniformity and certainty in the law. A judge following a precedent is bound by its underlying principle, not by the facts of the earlier case, so section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act is irrelevant to whether the precedent binds. The judicial oath likewise does not permit a judge to disregard precedent. The Court relied on Jaisri Sahu v. Rajdewan Dubey and Lala Shri Bhagwan v. Shri Ram Chand, among other authorities, and referred to Pinjare Karimbhai v. Shukla Hariprasad, Haridas v. Ratansey, and State of Gujarat v. Gordhandas.

predicates.single_judge_deciding_case: A single judge was deciding a case.
predicates.applicable_precedent_from_coordinate_or_: A relevant decision of a court of coordinate or superior authority applied to the case.

issues.definition: When a single judge decides a case to which an applicable precedent of coordinate or superior authority applies, the judge must follow that precedent.

issues.legal_issue: A larger-bench decision constituted by the Chief Justice following a judge’s request for reference is binding and cannot be disregarded as legally nonexistent because the request itself lacked authority.
material_facts: A judge requested that the case be placed before the Chief Justice so that a larger bench could be constituted to decide the legal question.
The Chief Justice constituted the larger bench, which considered and decided the question.
The single judge later treated the larger-bench decision as having no legal existence because the request for reference allegedly lacked authority.
issues.conclusion: A judge’s request to the Chief Justice to constitute a larger bench does not itself assume the Chief Justice’s powers; the Chief Justice constitutes the bench, and its duly delivered decision is binding. No constitutional or charter authority is required for the judge merely to make the request.
issues.legal_principle: When a judge or bench considers that conflicting decisions exist or an important question of law arises, the judge or bench may request that the papers be placed before the Chief Justice to constitute a larger bench. The Chief Justice, not the referring judge, constitutes the bench; the request is not the source of the bench’s authority. A decision delivered by the constituted Full Bench cannot be treated as irrelevant because of an alleged irregularity in the reference. The Court applied the principles on judicial propriety and binding precedent stated in Jaisri Sahu v. Rajdewan Dubey and Lala Shri Bhagwan v. Shri Ram Chand, and considered the Full Bench decision in State of Gujarat v. Gordhandas.

predicates.case_referred_for_larger_bench: A judge or bench requested that a case or legal question be considered by a larger bench.
predicates.chief_justice_constituted_larger_bench: The Chief Justice constituted the larger bench that heard and decided the matter.

issues.definition: When a case is requested for larger-bench consideration and the Chief Justice constitutes that bench, its decision is binding.
